name: Orforglipron
lead: Orforglipron (LY3502970), marketed as Foundayo, is a once-daily oral, non-peptide small-molecule agonist of the GLP-1 receptor developed by Eli Lilly for obesity and type 2 diabetes.[1] Unlike injectable peptide drugs such as semaglutide, it is a small molecule taken by mouth.

A phase 2 trial and a phase 3 trial in adults with obesity reported dose-related weight loss versus placebo over 72 weeks.[2][3] A US drug label states it is indicated, with diet and physical activity, to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related condition, and carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours that applies to the GLP-1 class.[4] Grokipedia reports FDA approval on April 1, 2026.[1]

paras: The US label lists chronic weight management in adults with obesity, or with overweight and at least one weight-related comorbid condition, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.[4] It has also been studied in type 2 diabetes.[5][6]

The phase 3 obesity trial randomised adults with obesity without diabetes to 6, 12 or 36 mg or placebo for 72 weeks as an adjunct to diet and activity.[3] Grokipedia reports weight reductions of up to 11.2% with the highest dose versus 2.1% with placebo in the ATTAIN-1 trial, which should be checked against the primary report.[1] In type 2 diabetes, phase 2 and phase 3 trials reported reductions in HbA1c and body weight.[5][6]

Gastrointestinal reactions such as nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting were reported as the most common events, more frequent during dose escalation.[1][2] The US label lists thyroid C-cell tumour risk, acute pancreatitis, severe gastrointestinal reactions, acute kidney injury from volume depletion, hypoglycaemia with certain co-medications, hypersensitivity and diabetic retinopathy complications as warnings. It notes that orforglipron is not pharmacologically active in rodents and did not produce rodent tumours, and that its relevance to humans is uncertain. It advises discontinuation in pregnancy.[4] A meta-analysis has compared the safety of oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonists.[7]

Orforglipron binds and activates the human GLP-1 receptor, a regulator of appetite and caloric intake.[4] A study in Science Translational Medicine described the structural basis of its non-peptide agonism.[8] Grokipedia describes it as a partial agonist biased toward cyclic AMP signalling.[1] Phase 1 studies tested single and multiple ascending doses in healthy participants and in type 2 diabetes.[9][10] Reported pharmacokinetics include oral bioavailability near 79% and CYP3A4 metabolism, from Grokipedia.[1]
Registered phase 3 trials examine orforglipron in obesity with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, peripheral artery disease, and overweight with risk of complications.[11][12][13][14]

Published human trials include phase 1 studies,[9][10] a phase 2 obesity trial,[2] a phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial,[5] a phase 3 trial in early type 2 diabetes,[6] and a phase 3 obesity trial.[3] Meta-analyses have pooled small-molecule GLP-1 agonists.[7][15]

timeline.event: Phase 3 results published in obesity and type 2 diabetes.[3][6]
Reported FDA approval as Foundayo (April 1, per Grokipedia).[1]

card.summary: Once-daily GLP-1 pill that isn't a peptide; phase 3 weight loss data and a US label, still newer than injectables.
card.note: Prescription-only with GLP-1-class warnings; boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning.

quick.overview:
Orforglipron is a once-daily pill from Eli Lilly that activates the GLP-1 receptor without being a peptide, so it needs no injection. It is sold in the US as Foundayo for chronic weight management.

Phase 2 and 3 trials reported dose-related weight loss versus placebo over 72 weeks in adults with obesity.
quick.mechanism: It binds and activates the human GLP-1 receptor, which regulates appetite and food intake.
quick.risks: Common effects are gastrointestinal. The label warns about thyroid C-cell tumours, pancreatitis, kidney injury and other effects, and advises stopping in pregnancy.
